pr.body:
We're adding one more step in the GitHub integration installation pipeline, namely GitHub OAuth2 authorize. This is transparent from the UX perspective as the data exchange happens without user interaction.

The pipeline will now fail in these cases:
- If there is a mismatch between currently authenticated GitHub user (derived from OAuth2 authorize step) and the user who installed the GitHub app (https://github.com/apps/sentry-io)
- If there is a mismatch between `state` parameter supplied by user and pipeline signature
- If GitHub could not generate correct `access_token` from the `code` (wrong or attempt of re-use of `code`).

In all those cases, this error is shown:
![image](https://github.com/getsentry/sentry/assets/1127549/18923861-2ead-4cf5-adda-7738aef801d7)
pr.title: fix(security): validate GitHub user during integration installation

raw_findings.body: The `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature` check only rejects accidental mismatches, not attackers. The PR's stated protection against forged installation requests (state mismatch detection) is ineffective: an attacker can pass the state check and inject their own OAuth code, binding `github_authenticated_user` to the attacker in the victim's pipeline (login CSRF / session fixation).
raw_findings.failure_mode: State validation passes for attacker-forged callbacks, defeating the anti-forgery goal of the security fix.
raw_findings.impact: The `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature` check only rejects accidental mismatches, not attackers. The PR's stated protection against forged installation requests (state mismatch detection) is ineffective: an attacker can pass the state check and inject their own OAuth code, binding `github_authenticated_user` to the attacker in the victim's pipeline (login CSRF / session fixation).
raw_findings.root_cause: The new OAuthLoginView reuses the deterministic, publicly-derivable pipeline signature as the OAuth state parameter instead of a per-session secret nonce.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Generate a cryptographically random per-pipeline nonce, bind it via `pipeline.bind_state("oauth_state", nonce)` before redirecting to GitHub, and compare the callback `state` against that stored nonce (constant-time), instead of the static pipeline signature.
raw_findings.title: OAuth 'state' is the constant pipeline signature, providing no CSRF/forgery protection
raw_findings.trigger: Any attacker can compute or observe the state value: Pipeline.signature is md5 of the pipeline view class paths (see pipeline/base.py `md5_text(*pipe_ids).hexdigest()`), so it is identical for every user and every session. The tests even hardcode the value "9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3". An attacker crafts a callback URL to /extensions/github/setup/ with the known state and their own `code`/`installation_id` and gets it loaded in a victim's browser mid-pipeline.

raw_findings.body: Unhandled KeyError raises a 500 server error instead of rendering the controlled github-integration-failed error page, breaking the installation flow for legitimate users with legacy integrations.
raw_findings.failure_mode: Runtime exception (KeyError) in the pipeline dispatch, surfacing as a 500 instead of the intended error response.
raw_findings.impact: Unhandled KeyError raises a 500 server error instead of rendering the controlled github-integration-failed error page, breaking the installation flow for legitimate users with legacy integrations.
raw_findings.root_cause: New sender-verification code assumes 'sender' is always present in Integration.metadata, but it is only conditionally populated by the webhook path.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and decide explicitly (error page or allow) when sender metadata is absent, rather than indexing directly.
raw_findings.title: KeyError when existing Integration lacks 'sender' metadata during sender-match check
raw_findings.trigger: A user re-installs against an ACTIVE Integration whose metadata has no 'sender' key — e.g., integrations created before this change, or created via `build_integration` without webhook state (`if state.get("sender")` only conditionally sets it; installation.py explicitly guards `if "sender" not in integration.metadata`).

raw_findings.body: A later legitimate callback without installation_id in the query string makes GitHubInstallation fall back to `pipeline.fetch_state("installation_id")`, resuming with the attacker's installation. If the attacker's Integration row does not yet exist (webhook race), the `Integration.DoesNotExist` branch advances the pipeline with no sender check, installing the attacker's GitHub installation into the victim's org.
raw_findings.failure_mode: Attacker-controlled installation_id survives a rejected request and poisons subsequent legitimate pipeline steps.
raw_findings.impact: A later legitimate callback without installation_id in the query string makes GitHubInstallation fall back to `pipeline.fetch_state("installation_id")`, resuming with the attacker's installation. If the attacker's Integration row does not yet exist (webhook race), the `Integration.DoesNotExist` branch advances the pipeline with no sender check, installing the attacker's GitHub installation into the victim's org.
raw_findings.root_cause: Unvalidated request input is persisted to durable pipeline state before the request's authenticity check runs.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Only bind installation_id on the initial (no-state) leg, or move the bind after the state parameter has been validated against the pipeline signature.
raw_findings.title: installation_id is bound to pipeline state before OAuth state validation
raw_findings.trigger: While a victim has an in-progress GitHub install pipeline, an attacker gets the victim's browser to request /extensions/github/setup/?installation_id=<attacker_id>&state=<anything>. The bind executes before the `state != pipeline.signature` check, so the attacker-controlled installation_id is persisted into the victim's pipeline state even though the request is rejected.

raw_findings.body: The 404-installation error path in `build_integration` (raising IntegrationError("The GitHub installation could not be found.")) loses all test coverage; the test name no longer matches what it verifies, so regressions in that path will go undetected while a state-mismatch check is duplicated.
raw_findings.evidence: assert b"Invalid installation request." in resp.content
raw_findings.failure_mode: Coverage regression: a named error path is untested and the test asserts an unrelated error message.
raw_findings.impact: The 404-installation error path in `build_integration` (raising IntegrationError("The GitHub installation could not be found.")) loses all test coverage; the test name no longer matches what it verifies, so regressions in that path will go undetected while a state-mismatch check is duplicated.
raw_findings.root_cause: The test was patched to satisfy the new two-step flow by sending a wrong state, silently changing which code path it covers.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Complete the OAuth leg with the correct state and valid mocked token exchange so the pipeline reaches get_installation_info and the mocked 404, then re-assert on "The GitHub installation could not be found."; keep the state-mismatch assertion in a separately named test.
raw_findings.title: test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the installation-not-found (404) path
raw_findings.trigger: Run test_installation_not_found: the second request deliberately sends a mismatched state ("ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05"), so the flow short-circuits at the OAuthLoginView state check and never reaches `get_installation_info`/the mocked 404, and the previous assertion on "The GitHub installation could not be found." was deleted.

finding.title: OAuth 'state' is the constant pipeline signature, providing no CSRF/forgery protection
finding.trigger: Any attacker can compute or observe the state value: Pipeline.signature is md5 of the pipeline view class paths (see pipeline/base.py `md5_text(*pipe_ids).hexdigest()`), so it is identical for every user and every session. The tests even hardcode the value "9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3". finding.verifier_reason: The claim that pipeline.signature is 'publicly-derivable' is incorrect. While the signature is deterministic based on pipeline view class paths, it is computed server-side and stored in the user's session (Redis). An attacker cannot compute it without knowing the exact module paths, and more importantly, the state parameter is tied to the user's session via PipelineSessionStore. The OAuth flow validates that the returning state matches the pipeline signature stored in that specific user's session, providing session-binding protection against CSRF.

finding.verifier_reason: The claim that installation_id persists after a rejected request is incorrect. Looking at the code flow: bind_state happens at line 399, but the state validation at line 412 only occurs when state parameter IS present. If an attacker sends a request with both installation_id and a wrong state, the request is rejected, but the pipeline state is session-bound. A subsequent legitimate request would go through the full OAuth flow with GitHub, getting a fresh code, and the installation_id would be re-bound from the legitimate callback. The attack scenario described is not realistic.
